newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian announces sell-offs but terms unclear.
newsitem.headline: Russian announces sell-offs but terms unclear.

text.p: New Russian plans to sell huge stakes in valuable oil companies announced on Thursday have raised questions whether the government will be able to sell the stakes freely and at a fair price.
The Federal Property Fund will sell 15 percent of Russia's biggest oil company LUKoil, 1.5-2.0 percent of national power company Unified Energy System (UES) and a large stake in Slavneft oil group.
Slavneft's major operating unit is Megionneftegaz. The Russian government owns about 84 percent of Slavneft and the Belarus government about nine percent.

Deputy Chairman Vladimir Malin said plans to sell 34 percent of oil group ONAKO, whose main operating company is Orenburgneft, had been put off until 1998 at the request of authorities in the region where it is based.
But he confirmed the fund intended to sell 50 percent of Russia's biggest insurance company Rosgosstrakh this year and an unspecified stake in Nafta-Moskva, a major Russian oil exporter.
In addition to the 15 percent stake in OAO Neftyanaya Kompaniya LUKoil, the fund is also considering selling an option on 4.5 percent of the company, he said.
Oil analysts said the Russian government was less likely or able to sell stakes in the companies concerned at below market prices than in the early days of privatisation.
"The market is too transparent to have a rip-off," said a Western oil and gas analyst, referring to the proposed LUKoil sale.
Stakes in major oil and natural resources companies were auctioned off at low prices in auctions in 1995 and 1996.
The proposals to sell off LUKoil could total almost 20 percent of the company, which has a market capitalisation of $10.7 billion.
Foreign investors will be watching the sale of LUKoil and other companies closely, said Stephen O'Sullivan, Associate Director of oil and gas at MC Securities.
He said that investors would not be surprised to see stakes go to insiders but that the government, companies and investors would all watch the price of sale closely.
"If it is an inside transaction, then investors may say, what is one more?" O'Sullivan said.
"The price to use is the price of shares on the Russian Trading System, and if it is different, they would have to show why."

The analysts said LUKoil's shares probably would go to domestic investors, although a LUKoil spokesman said the company's privatisation plan had intended the government share to be sold to foreign investors.
Such a move would sate part of the market for a forthcoming issue of American Depositary Receipts to raise new capital.
"The level-three ADR is easier to place if there is a broader market," said the Western oil analyst.

But whether to foreign or domestic investors, present management is unlikely to lose, or give up, control, the analysts said. Recent auctions have seen management or allies retain stakes in oil companies YUKOS and SIDANKO while the Communications Ministry has announced it will block foreign investors getting stragetic control of national telecoms holding company AO Svyazinvest in a forthcoming auction.
"If (LUKoil) goes to a Russian interest group, it is unlikely to go to a group who is not friendly to LUKoil," O'Sullivan said.
